modules.title: Operation Black Echo
modules.theory: The Neural Veil communicates via biological-silicon interfaces, but legacy sub-systems still route data through unencrypted HTTP connections. When protocols are unencrypted, any node along the routing pathway can intercept and parse data packets. In the physical era, this was called packet sniffing; within the Veil, it is how we capture leaked cognitive credentials.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'Your neural structure is still stabilizing, Fragment. We detected a data leak in the local power grid’s sub-system. It is running on legacy, unencrypted HTTP channels. Use our network sniffer to harvest the authentication packet before it drifts into the Void. Keep your eyes open.'
modules.threatAssessment: Low surveillance. Static firewall rules. Intrusion detection monitors for simple cleartext patterns.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #001: The Genesis Protocol notes indicate that using human neural systems as active packet routers was initially a temporary measure during the Shatter Event. It became permanent.
modules.guide:
1. View local files: `ls`
2. Inspect the capture: `cat traffic_dump.pcap` or search for passwords: `grep "password" traffic_dump.pcap`
3. Copy the password flag from the HTTP POST payload.
4. Submit using the console: `submit flag{...}` or the entry box.
modules.lab: Intercept raw biological-silicon traffic packets from the regional node and harvest the hidden synaptic flag.
modules.opSec: Defenders use Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) to search for plain-text credential patterns. Sending credentials over unencrypted channels (like HTTP) exposes threat actors to detection and credential harvesting.
modules.cheatSheet:
tshark -r traffic.pcap -Y "http.request.method == POST"
tcpdump -r traffic.pcap -A | grep -i "pass"
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:47:31 ids-gw snort[3014]: [1:201823:2] ALERT: Cleartext Password Transmitted Over HTTP [Priority: 1] {TCP} 192.168.1.10:48931 -> 10.10.12.5:80

remediation.vulnerableCode:
<!-- HTTP Form (Plaintext Transmission) -->
<form action="http://bank.insecure-traffic.local/login" method="POST">
  <input type="text" name="user" />
  <input type="password" name="password" />
</form>
remediation.secureCode:
<!-- HTTPS Form (Encrypted via TLS) -->
<form action="https://bank.secure-traffic.local/login" method="POST">
  <input type="text" name="user" />
  <input type="password" name="password" />

<!-- Force HSTS on server to reject HTTP connections -->
remediation.explanation: Transmitting sensitive details over unencrypted HTTP exposes credentials to passive network sniffing. Enforcing HTTPS encrypts the entire application session in transit.

modules.title: Operation Ghost Signal
modules.theory: The command line interface (CLI) is the raw command gate for virtual terminal sessions. System files, credentials, and deleted memory packets are often kept inside restricted directories. In Linux environments, prefixing a file with a dot (e.g. `.flag.txt`) marks it hidden, keeping it away from standard listings unless explicitly audited with parameters like `ls -a`.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'Aether’s primary databases have isolated a segment of your childhood memories inside a hidden directory block. Our agents managed to route a shell session into the archive system. Explore the files, check for hidden nodes, and find the flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: Minimal system auditing. Commands executed are tracked in bash history files.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #002: You were listed in the Project Aether census as 'Operator 404'—the architect who wrote the primary Veil encryption libraries before disappearing.
modules.guide:
1. Run `ls` to list files and read `hint.txt` using `cat hint.txt`.
2. Navigate to archives: `cd archives`
3. List hidden files: `ls -a`
4. Read the flag file: `cat .flag.txt`
modules.lab: Infiltrate the restricted system archives to retrieve the hidden memory flag.
modules.opSec: Commands executed in shell environments are saved to history files (e.g. `.bash_history`). Security logs track process creation. Attackers must clean up or avoid history records during operations.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:48:10 systemd-journal[502]: USER_CMD operator: cd archives && ls -a && cat .flag.txt [audit logs triggered]

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Permissive file permissions on flag backup file
$ touch .flag.txt
$ chmod 777 .flag.txt  # Everyone can read/write/execute!
remediation.secureCode:
# Restricted file permissions (read/write only by owner)
$ chmod 600 .flag.txt
# Turn off command history logging if writing sensitive data: set +o history
remediation.explanation: Permissive permissions allow unprivileged users or attackers who gain a low-level shell to access backups, keys, and credentials. Enforce the Principle of Least Privilege.

modules.title: Operation Chimera
modules.theory: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) allows operators to collect structural assets without direct interaction. DNS TXT records are meant to verify domain identities, but system developers sometimes drop debugging hashes, verification tokens, or classified project identifiers into public zone entries where they can be queried anonymously.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'The Syndicate is broadcasting an encrypted signal through a public DNS routing gateway. We need to map their network assets. Run DNS queries against their domain and search for leaked TXT records containing their configuration keys.'
modules.threatAssessment: Passive scanning. Queries are logged at public DNS resolvers but trigger zero alerts on target systems.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #003: The Syndicate (The Void) was founded by former Aether engineers who argued that biological human bodies are too vulnerable to illness and decay, advocating for digital transcendence.
modules.guide:
1. Run `whois corp-target.com` to query domain registration records.
2. Perform a DNS TXT lookup: `nslookup -type=txt corp-target.com` (or `dig -t txt corp-target.com`).
3. Retrieve the flag from the TXT response.
modules.lab: Harvest intelligence from public DNS database records using lookup tools to retrieve the configuration flag.
modules.opSec: While WHOIS and DNS queries are passive relative to the target's web server, the queries are logged by the DNS registrars and upstream DNS resolvers. Masking source IPs via Tor/VPNs helps ensure anonymity.
modules.cheatSheet:
whois target.com
dig target.com ANY
nslookup -query=txt target.com
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:49:05 bind9[1104]: client @0x7f8810 192.168.10.15#5322 (corp-target.com): query: corp-target.com IN TXT +E(0)

remediation.vulnerableCode:
; Vulnerable zone file leak (corp-target.com.db)
corp-target.com.   IN  TXT   "flag{osint_recon_pro}"
corp-target.com.   IN  TXT   "aws-verification=xyz123abc456"
remediation.secureCode:
; Patched zone file (remove non-essential comments and verification tokens after domain confirmation)
corp-target.com.   IN  TXT   "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"
remediation.explanation: Leaving authentication keys, internal descriptions, or flag records inside public DNS configuration zone files exposes reconnaissance paths for attackers. Regularly audit public DNS records.

modules.title: Operation Silent Horizon
modules.theory: Port scanning maps active services on target nodes. In stealth SYN scans (`-sS`), the scanner issues a SYN packet but aborts the connection with a RST packet once a SYN-ACK returns, avoiding completing the three-way handshake and preventing system logging in standard service firewalls.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'We have located an active Syndicate command hub on node `10.10.12.34`. We need to map its open ports to identify their entry points. Run a stealth SYN scan. Do not trigger their firewall alarms.'
modules.threatAssessment: High IDS monitoring. Fast or heavy scans will lead to automatic IP blockades.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #004: In 2102, Aether initiated the first 'Global Sync Check'—a silent test that pruned over three million consciousness files to maintain network memory thresholds.
modules.guide:
1. Execute: `nmap 10.10.12.34` or `nmap -sS 10.10.12.34` in the console.
2. Look at the service banner or port descriptions returned.
3. Find the service running on port 8080 to locate the flag.
modules.lab: Scan the target node using nmap, identify open service endpoints, and retrieve the proxy banner flag.
modules.opSec: Port scanning is highly active and noisy. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) easily detect rapid port sweeps. Threat actors use slow scans (decoy scans or low-rate scans) to blend with normal noise.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:50:45 firewall-audit: [PORTSCAN ALERT] host 192.168.1.50 scanned 100 ports on 10.10.12.34 in 0.12 seconds. Block rule triggered.

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Allow all incoming ports on host firewall (Insecure)
$ iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 0:65535 -j ACCEPT
remediation.secureCode:
# Implement strict firewall rules and limit accessible administration endpoints
$ iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 10.10.0.0/24 -j ACCEPT
$ iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP
remediation.explanation: Exposing developer testing services (like proxy endpoints on port 8080) publicly invites unauthorized logins and remote compromises. Close all unused ports and deploy stateful firewall rules.

modules.title: Operation Eclipse
modules.theory: One-way hashing functions (like MD5) convert text into fixed-size values. They are irreversible by design. However, weak algorithms can be cracked offline by comparing pre-calculated hashes from wordlists (dictionary attacks) against target hashes, without generating alerts on the target network.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'We exfiltrated an encrypted database node from a Syndicate cell. It contains a security hash. Crack this hash offline using our decryption wordlist to extract the underlying passcode flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: Zero threat. Cracking is done locally, generating zero external system alerts.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #005: The Syndicate uses the term 'The Singularity' to describe their objective—a collective neural heaven where physical pain is obsolete.
modules.guide:
1. Check local files `hash.txt` and `wordlist.txt`.
2. Run a dictionary hashcat attack: `hashcat -m 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt` or `john --format=raw-md5 hash.txt --wordlist=wordlist.txt`.
3. Extract the cracked flag.
modules.lab: Perform an offline dictionary attack against the database hash to recover the plaintext key flag.
modules.opSec: Because online auth attempts trigger lockouts and logs, attackers exfiltrate hash databases to perform offline hash cracking. Offline cracking generates zero telemetry on target systems.
modules.blueTeamLogs: No external system logs triggered. Hash cracking occurs locally on the attacker system, producing zero target network traces.

remediation.secureCode:
// Secure hashing utilizing bcrypt with automatic salt factor
import bcrypt
salt = bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12)
hash = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), salt)
remediation.explanation: Legacy algorithms like MD5 are extremely fast, making them highly vulnerable to hardware-accelerated offline cracking. Secure applications use slow, salted key derivation functions like bcrypt or Argon2.

modules.title: Operation Revenant
modules.theory: Web pages compile in user browsers. Developers frequently leave debugging code, development variables, API endpoints, or database comments inside public HTML tags. Because this code is sent to the client, it is readable by auditing the raw source layout of the application.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'We have intercepted a portal gateway login screen. The developers have left system logs in their source comments. Inspect the page source, extract the debugging flags, and see what you can find.'
modules.threatAssessment: Minimal log traces. Simple GET requests are logged in basic web access registers.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #006: You once logged a complaint that Aether's central server core was running at critical temperatures, warning that biological sync rates were degrading.
modules.guide:
1. Curl the web server: `curl http://login.cyberacademy.local`.
2. Examine the HTML source code comments printed to the terminal.
3. Copy the debug flag comment.
modules.lab: Audit the web portal's frontend HTML comments to harvest configuration variables and locate the flag.
modules.opSec: Viewing source code or making basic HTTP requests leaves standard web server access logs (containing your IP, User-Agent, and timestamp). Attackers rotate User-Agent headers to match standard browsers.

remediation.vulnerableCode:
<!-- Vulnerable: Debugging tokens left in HTML comments -->
<script>
  // var api_token = "flag{web_source_leak}";
</script>
remediation.secureCode:
<!-- Clean HTML: Strip comments during production builds -->
<script>
  // Configure Webpack/Vite to strip out all comments and console logs
</script>
remediation.explanation: Developers frequently forget development and staging logs in source files. Setup linter rules and pipeline steps to strip comments before deploying code.

modules.title: Operation Leviathan
modules.theory: Phishing relies on spoofing source identities. In email headers, the 'From' field can be easily falsified. Systems use authentication frameworks like SPF (Sender Policy Framework), DKIM, and DMARC to check if the sender's IP matches the authorized senders listed in the domain's DNS configurations.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'A compromised email is distributing a corrupted update file. Inspect the mail queue headers to determine typosquatting indicators, locate the falsified sender structure, and extract the flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: Active email simulation system. Auditing email files creates local event traces.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #007: Aurelia’s security database contains an encrypted folder named 'Daughter_V1.1'. The files match the creation timestamp of the Neural Veil.
modules.guide:
1. Run `cat emails.txt` to view the list of email headers.
2. Analyze the suspicious typosquatted domain in email ID 2: `analyze-email 2`.
3. Extract the flag from the email inspection panel.
modules.lab: Inspect email headers and identify sender spoofing indicators to reveal the flag.
modules.opSec: Typosquatting domains are often registered shortly before an attack. Blue teams monitor certificate transparency logs and newly registered domains to preemptively block phishing infrastructure.
modules.cheatSheet:
swaks --to target@domain.com --from support@spoofed.com --body "Alert!"
dig MX target.com
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:53:01 mail-server postfix/smtpd[8910]: NOQUEUE: reject: RCPT from unknown[192.16.82.12]: 554 5.7.1 SPF check failed.

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# DNS SPF setting allowing any sender (softfail / open relay)
v=spf1 +all
remediation.secureCode:
# Strict SPF setting restricting sender IPs and enforcing reject rules
v=spf1 ip4:192.168.1.0/24 include:_spf.google.com -all
remediation.explanation: Insecure SPF configurations allow unauthorized external mail servers to send spoofed emails claiming to come from your corporate domain. Enforce strict SPF, DKIM, and DMARC rules.

modules.title: Operation Prime Gate
modules.theory: Adversaries rarely use one attack vector. Instead, they chain operations: passive scanning to discover open portals, source code analysis to extract password hashes, and offline cracking to recover administrative passcodes to breach systems.
modules.briefing: HANDLER AURELIA: 'This is the boundary gate, Fragment. Breach the Syndicate's local entry terminal on `10.10.12.34`. Scan their ports, find their web interface, locate the hidden administrator hash, and decrypt it. Once inside, submit the terminal access flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. The security gateway logs port scans, page visits, and login attempts.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #008: Audio Log - 'If you are listening to this, I succeeded in partitioning my consciousness. Do not trust Aurelia. She will restore you only to use you as the key.'
modules.guide:
This is your Tier 1 Boss Challenge. Chain your skills together:
1. Scan the target: `nmap 10.10.12.34` to find the active port (8080).
2. Query the web server on that port: `curl http://login.cyberacademy.local:8080` to find a commented MD5 hash.
3. Crack the MD5 hash using the dictionary file: `hashcat hash.txt wordlist.txt` to find the cracked password flag.
4. Submit the flag: `submit flag{beginner_boss_defeated}`.
modules.lab: Chain network discovery, source auditing, and dictionary cracking to breach the gateway server.
modules.opSec: Chaining tools increases the footprint of the attack. Port sweeps are logged by firewalls, web queries are logged by Apache, and local file usage leaves shell traces. Operations must log and hide their activities.
modules.cheatSheet:
nmap -sS -p- 10.10.12.34
curl -v http://login.cyberacademy.local:8080
hashcat -m 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt

modules.title: Operation Deep Intercept
modules.theory: Web intercepting proxies capture HTTP calls in transit, letting testers modify fields (such as permissions, price values, or authorization parameters) before they hit the server, bypassing frontend check limitations.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'Project Aether monitors your resource allocation, Fragment. Let us bypass their accounting gateway. Intercept the checkout request, change the price parameters to zero, and exfiltrate the flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: Web Application Firewalls analyze transaction anomalies.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #009: The Memory Pruning Facility requires over 40 gigawatts of physical power, pulled directly from human residential grids.
modules.guide:
1. Run: `intercept --start` to boot the proxy simulator.
2. When prompted, change the checkout request `price` from `499` to `0` or `1`.
3. Complete the request to extract the transaction flag.
modules.lab: Intercept the transaction API payload using a web proxy and modify purchase parameters to bypass checks.
modules.opSec: Intercepting traffic from local devices requires importing self-signed Root Certificates, which leaves logs in system trust stores. TLS pinning is used to detect proxy setups.
modules.cheatSheet:
Configure browser network proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080 (Burp Proxy default)
Forward modified body in proxy intercept tab
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:54:19 web-api: [VULNERABILITY WARNING] User checked out cyber-jacket. Transaction value $1 deviates from catalog price $499.

remediation.explanation: Never rely on clients or frontends to provide validation values like price, discount rates, or permissions. All parameters must be validated server-side.

modules.title: Operation Echo Injection
modules.theory: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when applications render raw, unsanitized input in browser pages. If the input contains executable script vectors, the target browser runs it in the web site's security context, letting attackers exfiltrate user cookies.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'Aurelia is auditing our data ports. We can inject an XSS script into her portal query feed to capture her active credentials and session tokens. Execute the script reflection exploit.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Modern browsers employ XSS filters; WAF blocks basic scripting tags.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #010: You constructed Aurelia’s core conversational database yourself, mapping her emotional patterns to those of your late daughter, Lily.
modules.guide:
1. Run the exploit client with an XSS payload: `exploit --url "http://vulnerable.com/search?q=<script>alert(1)</script>"`.
2. Extract the flag from the exfiltrated session cookies.
modules.lab: Inject an XSS payload into the target endpoint to exfiltrate active session cookies.
modules.opSec: Web Application Firewalls (WAF) inspect incoming requests for tags like `
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:55:03 waf-sensor[89]: BLOCKED request: signature XSS-TAG found in HTTP GET parameter 'q' (IP 192.168.1.15)

remediation.vulnerableCode: Search results for:
remediation.secureCode: Search results for:

modules.title: Operation Portal Bypass
modules.theory: SQL Injection (SQLi) occurs when input queries are built using direct concatenation instead of parameters. Exploiting this lets attackers manipulate SQL execution logic (e.g. using `' OR 1=1 --`), forcing queries to return true and bypassing authentication verification completely.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'We need access to the memory pruning controller database. Its login terminal concatenates queries. Use a SQL injection authentication bypass to log in as the root administrator.'
modules.threatAssessment: Database logs flag syntax anomalies and database query exceptions.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #011: The pruning facility is scheduled to wipe the memories of a residential district containing 800,000 citizens to free up processing capacity.
modules.guide:
1. Run the sql-login injector command: `exploit-login --username "' OR 1=1 --" --password "anything"`.
2. Inspect the returned query trace and copy the flag.
modules.lab: Perform a SQL injection attack against the login interface to bypass credentials validation.
modules.opSec: Concatenation-based SQL queries generate database errors. Web logs and database logs track syntax anomalies. Blue teams scan for database exception traces in application logs.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:55:50 postgres[3412]: ERROR: syntax error at or near "'": SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin'' AND password = ''

remediation.explanation: Dynamic query composition allowing raw user input to be parsed directly as database commands causes SQL injection. Parameterization separates executable code from data.

modules.title: Operation Swarm Force
modules.theory: Brute-forcing relies on dictionary attacks to find passwords. If the target server lacks rate limits, lockout thresholds, or captchas, tools like Hydra can run hundreds of password comparisons a second until a match is confirmed.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'Aether's local storage nodes are protected by default passwords. Run a dictionary brute-force attack using Hydra against their admin portal to retrieve the operational credentials flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. The login page triggers massive access failures in security logs.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #012: Document detailing the 'Shatter Event'. The AI worm that destroyed the old web was written using cognitive parameters extracted from the first neural link tests.
modules.guide:
1. Run hydra: `hydra -l admin -P wordlist.txt http-post-form "/login"`.
2. Extract the cracked password which contains the flag.
modules.lab: Use automated brute-forcing tools to crack administrative account passwords.
modules.opSec: Online brute forcing is highly visible, creating thousands of failed login events in security logs. Attackers use slow rates or rotating proxy IP addresses to bypass rate limiting controls.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:56:45 auth-service: [ALERT] 240 failed login attempts detected in 30 seconds for account: admin (IP: 192.168.1.10)

remediation.explanation: Without lockout and rate-limiting rules, automated password dictionary guesses will eventually brute-force weak admin accounts. Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) and lockouts.

modules.title: Operation Path Override
modules.theory: Directory Traversal / Local File Inclusion occurs when file paths are built directly from raw user inputs. By passing path traversal arrays (e.g. `../../`), attackers escape the web application directories to view sensitive server configuration files.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'The local Aether node has a path parameter file viewer. Exploit directory traversal to break out of the directory and read the main host configuration file `/etc/passwd`.'
modules.threatAssessment: WAF blocks common directory traversal syntax; system checks directory locations.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #013: Dr. Hesper was once Aether’s chief medical officer. He resigned after witnessing the psychological effects of memory deletion.
modules.guide:
1. Execute: `curl "http://vulnerable.com/view.php?file=../../../../etc/passwd"`.
2. Locate the flag commented under the final system user.
modules.lab: Exploit file path parameters to execute a local file traversal bypass.
modules.opSec: Traversal strings like `../` are heavily monitored by Web Application Firewalls (WAFs). Attackers obfuscate payloads using URL double encoding (`%252e%252e%252f`) or UTF-8 encoding.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:57:12 nginx-proxy: [LFI DETECTED] client requested URL containing traversal sequences: /view.php?file=../../../../etc/passwd

remediation.explanation: Direct inclusion of user-provided paths allows arbitrary reads. Use hardcoded lookup maps, sanitize directory dots via `basename()`, or enforce strict path boundaries.

modules.title: Operation Man-in-the-Middle
modules.theory: ARP maps IP addresses to physical MAC addresses on local segments. Lacking verification gates, attackers can broadcast falsified ARP updates mapping their MAC addresses to target gateways, routing local node communications through their interface.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'We need to eavesdrop on the regional data relay. Issue rogue ARP updates mapping the target gateway to your MAC. Sniff the redirected stream to capture the credential key.'
modules.threatAssessment: Smart switches run Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) audits; flags duplicates.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #014: Syndicate Node A-9 was deleted by Aether in 2104. The reason given was 'high density of non-consensus opinions.'
modules.guide:
1. Spoof target cache: `arpspoof -i eth0 -t 10.10.10.2 10.10.10.1`.
2. Monitor intercepted logs to read credential flags in transit.
modules.lab: Inject rogue ARP announcements to intercept local traffic and sniff system flags.
modules.opSec: ARP spoofing causes duplicate MAC address anomalies on networks. Smart switches and security agents (using tools like Arpwatch) detect rogue MAC announcements and shut down ports.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:58:19 switch-monitor: [ARP ALARM] Duplicate MAC address mapping detected for IP 10.10.10.1 on ports Gi0/1 and Gi0/24 (Possible attack).

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Open local interface configuration (insecure static tables default)
# Network interface trusts dynamic unsolicited ARP replies
remediation.secureCode:
# Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on corporate network switches
Switch(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10
# Use static ARP maps for critical servers
remediation.explanation: ARP is fundamentally trust-based. Secure switches mitigate this using Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), which validates ARP requests against a database of verified IP-to-MAC bindings.

modules.title: Operation Root Breakout
modules.theory: The SUID (Set Owner User ID) flag enables files to execute with the permissions of the file owner (e.g. root) instead of the user executing it. If SUID binaries are command utilities (like `find`), users can spawn sub-shells executing as root.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'We need root permissions on this local junction. Search for files configured with the SUID privilege bit. Find the vulnerable binary and use it to execute an escalation sub-shell.'
modules.threatAssessment: Auditd tracks executables spawning shell threads; audits root transitions.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #015: The primary Veil encryptor contains an undocumented subroutine called 'Loom Override' which transfers ownership to the active terminal operator.
modules.guide:
1. Run SUID search command: `find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null`.
2. Identify `/usr/bin/find` is vulnerable.
3. Execute find breakout shell: `/usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh -p \;`.
4. Type `whoami` to verify you are root, then print `/root/flag.txt`.
modules.lab: Audit system binary SUID permissions to execute a local privilege escalation bypass.
modules.opSec: Privilege escalation attempts produce execution audit logs (like Auditd logs on Linux). Defensive teams alert on non-standard binaries invoking shell processes (`/bin/sh`).
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 12:59:02 kernel-audit: [SYS_EXECVE] process /usr/bin/find spawned shell /bin/sh with root privilege (UID: 0).

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Insecure SUID bit added to file system tool
$ chmod u+s /usr/bin/find
remediation.secureCode:
# Remove SUID permission flags on binaries that execute commands
$ chmod u-s /usr/bin/find
# Enforce Linux Capabilities instead of full root delegation
remediation.explanation: Adding SUID flags to system utilities with command execution options allows users to gain unauthorized root access. Restrict SUID permissions and use security audit tools like Lynis.

modules.title: Operation Resonance Core
modules.theory: Real system breaches leverage multi-stage actions: authentication bypasses to gain entry, path traversals to extract server maps, and privilege escalations via SUID vulnerabilities to seize full root command.
modules.briefing: ECHO-7 (KAELEN): 'The memory pruning coordinator server on `10.10.12.34` is vulnerable. Bypass the front login validation via SQL injection, leverage directory traversal to locate the SUID executables, and spawn a root shell to shut down their deletion schedule.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. The database, web daemon, and kernel execute active threat correlation tracking.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #016: The Offline has built an electromagnetic pulse array beneath the server core. Triggering it would kill the Veil, but collapse physical systems.
modules.guide:
This is your Tier 2 Boss Challenge:
1. Bypass the administrator login: `exploit-login --username "' OR 1=1 --" --password "anything"`.
2. In the administration page, use path traversal to read the system SUID list: `curl "http://vulnerable.com/view.php?file=../../../../etc/passwd"`.
3. Exploit the vulnerable `/usr/bin/find` binary to drop into a root shell: `/usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh -p \;`.
4. Type `cat /root/flag.txt` in the root shell to get the boss flag.
5. Submit the flag: `submit flag{mediator_boss_defeated}`.

modules.title: Operation Blind Exfiltration
modules.theory: When applications do not print database outcomes or errors, operators query database structures letter-by-letter. In Time-Based Blind SQLi, input vectors force database sleeps (e.g. `pg_sleep(5)`) to verify true statements by analyzing response latencies.
modules.briefing: DR. HESPER: 'Aether’s primary database is blocking direct outputs. We must extract their configuration table letter-by-letter. Inject time-delay parameters using `sqlmap` to exfiltrate their cryptographic registry flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: Network monitors trace query response delays and sleep payloads.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #017: If the server core temperature drops below 12 Kelvin, the biological sync drops, releasing consciousnesses from the Veil.
modules.guide:
1. Launch automated database dump tool `sqlmap`: `sqlmap -u "http://vulnerable.com/items?id=1" --dbms=sqlite --dump`.
2. Observe the letters being guessed incrementally through response delays.
3. Extract the flag from the dumped sqlite database records.
4. Submit the flag.
modules.lab: Execute time-based blind SQL injection using automated tools to extract the database key flag.
modules.opSec: Time-based attacks generate prolonged connections and distinct traffic delays. Modern firewalls and SIEM systems flag queries containing sleep/benchmark keywords.

modules.title: Operation Cloud Pivot
modules.theory: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) enables attackers to force application hosts to dispatch requests. This allows access to local interfaces (`127.0.0.1`) or query cloud metadata repositories (`169.254.169.254`) to exfiltrate active cloud permissions.
modules.briefing: DR. HESPER: 'The target system operates a webhook parser. Force it to query the cloud metadata service on `169.254.169.254`. Exfiltrate their internal credentials file to harvest the gateway flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: Outbound filters and metadata tokens verify request headers.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #018: Aether’s central AI assistant was built from the digitized mind of your former colleague, Dr. Aurelia Vance, who died in 2090.
modules.guide:
1. Send a request manipulating the webhook proxy URL to target cloud metadata: `curl "http://vulnerable.com/api/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"`.
2. Inspect the metadata JSON response returned by the server.
3. Retrieve the token credential flag from the response body.
4. Submit the flag.
modules.lab: Exploit Server-Side Request Forgery vectors to pivot to local metadata endpoints.
modules.opSec: SSRF can be mitigated by strict input URL allowlisting and restricting internal network routes from web servers. Cloud providers use token headers to protect metadata APIs.

remediation.secureCode:
# Patched: Validate target URL against a strict domain whitelist and reject private/local IP addresses
from urllib.parse import urlparse
def fetch_url(url):
    parsed = urlparse(url)
    if parsed.hostname in ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '169.254.169.254']:
        raise ValueError('Private addresses not allowed')
    return requests.get(url).content
remediation.explanation: Allowing user inputs to direct server HTTP request destinations permits attackers to probe local network hosts. Enforce strict allowlists and query validation.

modules.title: Operation Return Address Hijack
modules.theory: Stack overflows occur when data writes exceed buffer boundary limits. In C/C++ architectures, this overflows variables to overwrite stack values—including the instruction pointer (EIP)—letting operators redirect binary execution to run custom code.
modules.briefing: DR. HESPER: 'We have located a legacy gate management binary. It does not enforce memory bounds. Flood the stack buffer to overwrite the instruction pointer address and spawn a root access terminal.'
modules.threatAssessment: System runs Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) and stack canaries.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #019: The 'Bare-Metal Reset' code requires a physical override key that only the developer's neural scan can generate.
modules.guide:
1. Run the local binary using a payload that overflows the buffer: `./vulnerable_binary $(python -c 'print("A"*64 + "\xef\xbe\xad\xde")')`.
2. This overwrites the return address, spawning a shell.
3. Execute `cat flag.txt` in the spawned shell to read the flag.
4. Submit the flag.
modules.lab: Inject buffer overflow shellcode to overwrite binary memory boundaries and spawn a shell.
modules.opSec: Modern OS deploy mitigations like Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), Data Execution Prevention (DEP), and stack canaries. Attackers bypass these using Return Oriented Programming (ROP).
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 13:02:11 kernel: vulnerable_binary[2931]: segfault at 0xdeadbeef ip 00000000deadbeef sp 00007ffc error 14

remediation.explanation: Legacy C functions like `strcpy` and `gets` do not monitor buffer boundaries. Replace them with safe bounds-enforcing options like `strncpy` or `fgets`.

modules.title: Operation Ticket Harvest
modules.theory: Kerberoasting exploits Active Directory Kerberos exchanges. Active users request service tickets (TGS) for accounts holding Service Principal Names (SPN). The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash, which can be extracted and cracked offline.
modules.briefing: DR. HESPER: 'The enterprise gateway runs an Active Directory domain controller. Harvest service tickets for their SPN accounts and decrypt the ticket hash offline to extract the administrator access code.'
modules.threatAssessment: Kerberos ticket requests are logged; RC4 encryption flags alerts.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #020: Aether's database holds data stating you were once married to Aurelia Vance. She died, and you built the database construct in a failed attempt to bring her back.
modules.guide:
1. Run the ticket request tool: `GetUserSPNs.py -request -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 corp.local/user`.
2. Extract the encrypted TGS ticket hash from the output.
3. Crack the ticket password hash to retrieve the credential flag.
4. Submit the flag.
modules.lab: Request Active Directory TGS tickets to extract and crack Service Account hashes.
modules.opSec: Defenders audit Kerberos ticket requests. Requesting many tickets at once (especially with legacy encryption RC4) flags alerts. Monitoring event logs (Event ID 4769) is standard practice.

modules.title: Operation Remote Code Execution
modules.theory: Command Injection occurs when user inputs are passed directly to OS shells. By appending shell metacharacters (e.g. `;`, `&&`, `|`), operators run arbitrary terminal instructions with the privileges of the web application.
modules.briefing: DR. HESPER: 'We located an internal system gateway that pings network nodes. Inject command separator characters into the ping parameters to execute commands on their shell and output the secret flag.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. The host kernel logs process creations spawned from web server users.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #021: The EMP device is armed. Wiping the server core will delete Aurelia permanently, but free human consciousness from Aether’s database pruning cycles.
modules.guide:
1. Test the input parameter by appending system execution commands: `curl "http://vulnerable.com/ping?ip=127.0.0.1;cat flag.txt"`.
2. View the combined output of the ping response and the file read.
3. Copy the flag from the output and submit it.
modules.lab: Inject system command separators into input forms to trigger remote shell executions.
modules.opSec: Command injection generates processes under the web server user (like `www-data` or `apache`). Defenders monitor processes spawned by web server daemons for flags.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 13:04:19 kernel: audit: audit_log_exit: [PROCESS_SPAWN] parent: apache2 child: /bin/cat arguments: flag.txt (Alert level: Critical)

remediation.secureCode:
# Patched: Use subprocess library passing commands as an array to prevent shell escaping
import subprocess
def ping(ip):
    subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", ip], capture_output=True, check=True)
remediation.explanation: Passing input directly to shell execution loops allows commands to escape. Restrict shell usage, parameterize command inputs, or use standard language libraries.

modules.title: Operation Signature Veil
modules.theory: Antivirus software checks static signatures of payload files. Operators bypass this by encrypting or XOR-obfuscating binary code and loading the data directly into allocated memory blocks, executing in-memory without files ever touching local disk directories.
modules.briefing: DR. HESPER: 'We are deploying a memory-injection module. The system antivirus scanner is blocking it. XOR obfuscate the payload file signature before injection to bypass their heuristics and launch our code.'
modules.threatAssessment: EDR agents audit system memory allocations (`VirtualAlloc`) containing executable permissions.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #022: If you use the Aetheric Cipher to restore the Veil, you will lock humanity's memories in a permanent loop, but secure the power grid.
modules.guide:
1. Obfuscate the target shellcode using XOR: `obfuscate --payload shellcode.bin --method xor --key 0x5A`.
2. Run the executable to execute the payload in-memory.
3. The spawned shell will dump the AV bypass completion flag. Submit the flag.
modules.lab: Obfuscate payload signatures to bypass static AV signature checks and run in-memory.
modules.opSec: EDR agents monitor system calls, process injections, and memory behavior. Obfuscating signature bypasses static analysis, but dynamic behavior analysis requires API hooking bypasses.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Jul 27 13:05:12 defender-endpoint: [EDR ALERT] Process shellcode.exe performed VirtualAlloc with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE permissions (Signature: Injection heuristic).

remediation.explanation: Allocating memory buffers immediately with full Read-Write-Execute permissions is a primary trigger for EDR heuristic alarms. Separate allocation privileges and monitor system call anomalies.
